passages.label: A
passages.text: An older resident may be able to get to a leisure centre in theory, while a missing seat or hard-to-read timetable changes what happens on an actual trip. To understand such barriers, the World Health Organization consulted older people, caregivers and service providers in 33 cities across 22 countries. The documented problems gave councils specific issues to address. Measures including the median age and the proportion of older residents describe a demographic pattern, while people’s accounts show where services need to adapt.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Transport and outdoor space affect whether a person can reach shops, services and friends. An affordable bus is useful only if its schedule and destinations fit daily life. Safe crossings, public seating and accessible toilets can make a journey possible. Communities may need to adapt routes, signs or buildings for residents with limited mobility or vision. These changes are connected. A person may have somewhere valuable to go, yet stay home if the path or service is unsafe. Better mobility can therefore reduce isolation as well as improve practical access.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Housing and communication require choice rather than one standard solution. People may need a range of homes near services, from ordinary houses with small modifications to housing with more support. Information also needs several formats because not everyone uses a smartphone or reads a long notice easily. Clear printed material, telephone contact and accessible digital information can work together. Affordability matters too. A service that exists but costs more than a resident can pay is not fully accessible, whether the money comes from wages, savings or a pension.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Social participation includes cultural, educational, spiritual and leisure activities. Suitable times, locations and prices help people take part. The framework also values paid work, civic activity and voluntary roles, but contribution should remain a choice. An older resident may want to share professional experience, learn a new skill or simply meet neighbours. Respect is visible when organisers ask what people value instead of assuming that age defines their interests. A busy calendar alone does not create inclusion if transport, cost or an unwelcoming attitude keeps some residents away.

passages.label: E
passages.text: WHO guidance says that age-friendly work begins with local evidence and the voices of older people. A council can focus on barriers that residents actually experience, set priorities, name responsible partners and decide how progress will be measured. Local organisations may undertake different parts of the plan. By comparison, a national programme can connect communities and provide technical or financial support. Monitoring matters because a new bench, route or information service may work differently in practice than planners expected. Residents should be involved again when results are reviewed. To help residents cope with gaps in service, check the range of travel options and the capacity of each.

passages.label: F
passages.text: A council can estimate how many residents are capable of reaching a service without help and propose changes for those who are dependent on it. Local groups can cooperate and participate in a trial to assist people who travel alone. The responsibility for a path or bus stop matters. A council needs to know who can alter it. Removing a small barrier can enable a person in retirement to make a regular trip, while experience from one generation can inform decisions for the next.

R_H2.passageTitle: Two Routes Through a Senior Nutrition Service

passages.label: A
passages.text: Nutrition services supported through the Older Americans Act have four documented purposes: reducing hunger and food insecurity, encouraging social contact, supporting health and delaying harmful health conditions. Grants help states provide services through local ageing networks, and the programmes do more than distribute food. They connect meals with nutrition knowledge and other community support. Need varies, so providers must focus on older adults whose independence may be at risk. The national framework sets purposes, while local organisations decide how to deliver suitable services in their communities.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The Congregate Nutrition Program, established in 1972, serves meals in group settings such as senior centres and faith-based locations, and each meal provides at least one-third of recommended dietary reference intakes. The shared setting also creates opportunities for conversation, health activities and meaningful voluntary roles, and a participant may eat, meet neighbours and join an activity during the same visit. The social part is not an accidental extra, and it is one of the programme's stated purposes, although each local site can arrange its schedule and activities differently.

passages.label: C
passages.text: In contrast, the Home-Delivered Nutrition Program, established in 1978, takes meals to homebound older adults, and a delivery is often the initial in-home service a person receives. Volunteers and paid staff may also make an informal safety check and spend time with the individual, and the visit is not a clinical examination, but it can become a first link to other help. Home delivery allows a person who cannot reach a group site to receive food while remaining in the community, and it can also help reduce feelings of isolation.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Both routes connect people with a range of nutrition services, and these include screening, assessment, education and counselling. The ageing network can also link participants to transport, physical-activity programmes, chronic-disease self-management, home repair, home modification and falls prevention. Such connections matter when a person must cope with more than one difficulty at once. A meal alone cannot repair an unsafe step or arrange a medical appointment. A coordinated local network can notice a need and direct the person towards an appropriate service.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Capacity depends on kitchens, vehicles and staff who can undertake different jobs. Some people give their time on a voluntary basis. A service that could cover an area in theory may have to adapt routes to reach more residents in practice. The pattern of leisure and the geographic range of each service also matter. Local planners may compare the proportion of older residents who live alone or depend largely on a pension. They can then choose what to focus on as demographic conditions change. Each route needs a plan that people can use regularly.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Residents who participate in meals after retirement may be fully capable of travelling, or they may be dependent on support. Staff need to estimate how many people each service can assist, and whether kitchen and transport teams can cooperate. Providers may alter routes to enable delivery, while an indoor meeting place can ensure that people eating together have time to talk. The responsibility for staffing each route affects what services are practical in a particular neighbourhood.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Tanzania has made documented progress in child survival. Fertility has fallen more slowly, and a high proportion of people remain young. In demographic analysis, median age divides a population into two groups of equal size, and it is one useful measure, but it cannot describe the capacity of schools or employers. In theory, a larger working-age share can support faster growth. Understanding when that happens requires evidence about whether institutions can adapt as young people move through school and into work.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Rapid growth places pressure on public services. More children require classrooms, teachers, clinics, water and transport. If family size remains high, the World Bank projects that public education costs could rise from 3.3 per cent to 4.1 per cent of gross domestic product by 2061. That change may look small in percentage points, but it represents a larger claim on national resources. Institutions must expand their capacity if they are to cope with demand while maintaining service quality and reaching poorer or remote communities.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A youthful age structure can also create an economic opportunity when a larger share of people enters working age, and the benefit is not automatic. Young adults need useful skills and productive employment that provides a way to earn an income. Recent World Bank reporting on Africa says that the region creates fewer formal positions each year than the number of young people entering the labour force. Tanzania therefore needs a range of routes into economic activity, including growing firms, farms and small enterprises. Policy must focus on productivity and pay, not only the number of activities described as economic activity.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The demographic dividend refers to a potential increase in economic output as better health and declining fertility allow the working-age share of the population to rise. If learning and employment fail to expand, a large youth population can instead increase pressure on households and public institutions. Investment in girls and women matters because their health, education and ability to make decisions influence both family choices and the skills available to the economy. Realising the potential gain therefore depends on productive employment as well as a favourable change in population structure.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Health agencies, schools, trainers and employers may each undertake part of the response. A rise in the proportion of young adults can yield an advantage under a range of conditions, including access to training and paid employment. In contrast, where those opportunities expand slowly, families may have to cope with a longer wait for work. To sum up the argument in brief, age structure helps identify a potential opportunity. The opportunity becomes easier to assess when data focus on what young people can actually do next.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Public agencies can estimate the number of people reaching working age and calculate a rate of employment, while that evidence may indicate how well training is reaching a generation. Ministers can propose a new phase of education to enable learners to participate in work. Agencies that attempt to link training with work can cooperate and specify who has responsibility for each part. Skills can become an asset when the economy also offers ways for people to use them.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What can the median age show, and what is beyond that measure?
options: It shows the exact number of future jobs, but no fact about age.
It measures whether young adults already have all the skills employers need.
It locates the middle of the age distribution but does not show whether services or jobs can keep up.
It tells how much the country must spend per child instead of describing the population.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the projection from 3.3 to 4.1 per cent illustrate?
options: Education could require a greater share of national resources if family size stays high.
The percentage represents a past drop in the number of school places.
The new percentage is an employment rate expected for remote areas.
The figures prove costs will rise regardless of what happens to family size.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What distinction matters when looking at work for young adults?
options: Any activity measured by an agency gives the same benefit as a well-paid job.
Farm work is the sole work mentioned as being excluded from the economy.
There is no need to consider the amount of work or what it pays.
It matters what people can earn and produce, as well as whether an activity exists.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why is the demographic dividend described as potential?
options: It occurs once the number of younger people becomes smaller, regardless of employment.
A change in the working-age share can help, but the gain also depends on education and productive work.
It can be measured by counting the percentage of household spending that goes to clinics.
It results whenever a country's labour force receives a new name.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How does the passage link investment in girls and women with the wider argument?
options: It changes only the number of people in a remote area.
It removes the need for jobs or access to training.
It matters only after every public institution already has enough capacity.
Health, education and decision-making can affect families and the skills people can bring to the economy.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How could schools and employers use evidence to tell whether there is a gain rather than just a larger working-age group?
options: Use the median age by itself as a complete account of training and work.
Check whether training reaches young people and how many actually find work where they can use their skills.
Assume every additional person who reaches working age has found a productive job.
Count only the number of institutions mentioned in a national report.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What could happen when institutions cannot keep up with a rapidly growing young population?
options: Growing demand makes public service capacity unnecessary.
Larger youth cohorts guarantee higher earnings before entering the labour force.
Schools or clinics can face pressure and families may wait longer for work opportunities.
A larger share of children lowers education demand even if services do not expand.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What division of work does the text suggest for institutions responding to the change?
options: Different groups can take responsibility for distinct tasks and work together to connect training with employment.
Employers alone determine everything from school capacity to the results of training.
Agencies can ignore which body handles a step as long as they all make a proposal.
Each institution has to perform exactly the same job and use the same measures.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What would be a weakness in counting only new employment opportunities when judging the country's response?
options: A positive count proves that services, wages and skills have all improved.
New opportunities make it impossible to measure the use of skills.
Any formal job published by a company gives a complete national measure by itself.
A count does not establish whether people can develop the skills to enter the jobs, what they can produce there or what they can earn.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion makes sense of both public demands and later opportunities described in the passage?
options: Every rise in the number of young people becomes an economic advantage without investment.
Trends affect demand for services now, and a larger working-age share can help later if learning and productive jobs expand.
The best response is to track the changing age structure without examining what institutions do.
Higher spending on education cannot matter to any outcome once a region has young workers.
